## Bringing in the Grad_Admissions data into code, and a little exploring of the data.

I had to first bring the CSV file into my Assignment_9 folder, then I used the read.csv command to allow me to manipulate the file in R. I then looked at the summary data.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
Grad_Admins <- read.csv("GradSchool_Admissions.csv")
#Exploring the Dataset
head(Grad_Admins)
str(Grad_Admins)
summary(Grad_Admins)
```

## Looking for missing values & comparing existing values

After looking at the data from the code seen above, I checked for any missing values. I then compared the GRE and GPA of the students that applied and the percentage from being accept or not.

```{r}
#Checking missing values
colSums(is.na(Grad_Admins))
# Calculate admission percentages
prop.table(table(Grad_Admins$admit)) * 100
# Compare GRE and GPA by admission outcome
Grad_Admins %>%
  group_by(admit) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_GRE = mean(gre),
    Mean_GPA = mean(gpa),
    Number_of_Applicants = n()
  )
```

## Visualizing the data

The Code that I had used to generate the graphs is below, and the graphs are skewed to the left of each graph. There are more higher ranking students that are accepted than any other student rank.

```{r}

# Visualize GPA
ggplot(Grad_Admins, aes(x = gpa, fill = factor(admit))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "GPA by Admission Outcome",
    x = "GPA",
    y = "Number of Applicants",
    fill = "Admitted"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Admission rates by institution rank
rank_summary <- Grad_Admins %>%
  group_by(rank) %>%
  summarise(
    Applicants = n(),
    Accepted = sum(admit),
    Admission_Rate = mean(admit) * 100
  )

print(rank_summary)

# Plot admission rates by rank
ggplot(rank_summary,
       aes(x = factor(rank), y = Admission_Rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Admission Rate by Institution Rank",
    x = "Institution Rank",
    y = "Admission Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Visualize GRE scores
ggplot(Grad_Admins, aes(x = gre, fill = factor(admit))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "GRE Scores by Admission Outcome",
    x = "GRE Score",
    y = "Number of Applicants",
    fill = "Admitted"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Logistic Regression of the Data

After looking at the graphs of the Admission data, I used a quadratic fit for the data, and the Percent similarity to the data is very strong.

```{r}

# ==========================================
# LOGISTIC REGRESSION MODEL
# ==========================================

# Convert rank into a categorical variable
Grad_Admins$rank <- as.factor(Grad_Admins$rank)

# Fit logistic regression
mod1 <- glm(
  admit ~ I(gre / 100) + I(gpa * 10) + rank,
  data = Grad_Admins,
  family = binomial
)

# Examine model results
summary(mod1)

# Calculate odds ratios
exp(coef(mod1))

# Calculate confidence intervals
exp(confint(mod1))

# Model predictions
Grad_Admins$predicted_probability <- predict(
  mod1,
  type = "response"
)

# View predicted probabilities
head(Grad_Admins)
```

## Predicting using an example applicant with visualization

For predicting an outcome from the Data, I had created an example applicant, and had put their data into the model, and the visual probabilities in relation to the data is below.

```{r}
# Example applicant
new_applicant <- data.frame(
  gre = 600,
  gpa = 3.5,
  rank = factor(1, levels = levels(Grad_Admins$rank))
)

predict(
  mod1,
  newdata = new_applicant,
  type = "response"
)
# Visualize predicted probabilities
ggplot(Grad_Admins,
       aes(x = predicted_probability,
           fill = factor(admit))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Admission Probabilities",
    x = "Predicted Probability of Admission",
    y = "Number of Applicants",
    fill = "Actual Admission"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
